topics.title: Autonomous Hill Councils Ladakh
bullets: On 13 July 2026, the Ladakh Administration announced the constitution of an Autonomous Hill Development Council (AHDC) in each of the Union Territory's seven districts.
The decision extends the existing framework of elected local self- governance beyond the previous two districts of Leh and Kargil to the five new districts.
Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra described the move as a major step towards democratic decentralisation and grassroots governance. Background –
Ladakh was carved out as a separate Union Territory on 31 October 2019.
This followed the abrogation of Article 370 and the enactment of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act.
Unlike other Union Territories, Ladakh was created without a legislature, and is governed directly by the Centre through a Lieutenant Governor.
Since 2019, local groups have persistently demanded greater democratic representation, statehood, and constitutional safeguards.
Before 1995, Ladakh (then part of Jammu and Kashmir) had no dedicated elected local body.
In October 1993, the Union Government and the Jammu & Kashmir State Government reached an agreement to grant each district of Ladakh the status of an Autonomous Hill Council.
The LAHDC Act was promulgated in 1995 under the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils Act, 1995.
The Act provided the legal framework for the establishment of Autonomous Hill Development Councils and an Inter-District Advisory Council in the Ladakh region.
While the Act came into effect retrospectively from 1 June 1995, it was formally approved by the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly in 1997.
The first LAHDC (for Leh) was sworn in on 3 September 1995.
The Kargil council was constituted later in 2003 as part of a 'healing touch policy' following the Kargil conflict.
These councils were established to address the region's distinct needs and promote decentralized administration in the geographically remote hill areas.

After Ladakh became a UT in 2019, groups like the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) came together to jointly demand statehood, inclusion in the Sixth Schedule, a separate Public Service Commission, and dedicated Lok Sabha seats.
The Sixth Schedule demand was aimed at securing greater control over land and natural resources.
Activists like Sonam Wangchuk have been prominent voices in these protests, and he spent nearly six months in jail following protests in 2025.
In August 2024, the Ministry of Home Affairs approved the formation of five new districts.
The five new districts – Nubra, Sham, Changthang, Zanskar, and Drass – were finally made operational in April 2026.
This reorganisation increased the total number of districts in Ladakh from two to seven.
Three new districts – Nubra, Sham, and Changthang – were carved out from the Leh district.
Two new districts – Zanskar and Drass – were carved out from the Kargil district.
This administrative reorganisation was aimed at improving governance and development in remote areas, reducing travel distances for citizens often exceeding 300 km.
Following the district reorganisation, the administration also created 17 new tehsils, bringing the total number of tehsils in Ladakh to 32 from the previous 15.
Four new divisions under the Public Health Engineering (PHE) Department and five new divisions under the Public Works Department (PWD) were set up for high-altitude service delivery. Recent News –
AHDCs are democratically elected local self-governing bodies established to promote decentralized administration in geographically remote and culturally distinct hill regions.
They function as an intermediate tier between the district administration and the Union Territory administration.
Each Hill Council typically consists of 26 Councillors (22 directly elected and 4 nominated by the Lieutenant Governor).
The LAHDC Act provides for a council in every district, to be constituted from a date the government notifies in the gazette.
The councils function as statutory bodies created by an Act of the legislature, as opposed to the constitutional bodies under the Sixth Schedule.
The existing councils in Leh and Kargil had 30 members each (26 elected plus four nominated).
Chief Secretary Kundra has clarified that each of the seven Councils will carry the full powers set out in the LAHDC Act.
The new districts will get the same authority that Leh has held since 1995 and Kargil since 2003, not a reduced version of it.
This ensures that the newly created councils are not disadvantaged compared to the older ones.
The legal basis for this expansion already exists in Section 3(1) of the LAHDC Act, which provides for a council in every district.
Only amendments to the Act, where required, and delimitation of constituencies remain before the new Councils can be constituted.
This legal provision means that no fresh law is strictly required to create the councils, only amendments and notifications.
The Hill Councils will have authority over land ownership and land allotment within their respective districts.
They will regulate recruitment and promotion for district cadre posts.
Employment decisions in the new districts will rest with an elected body inside the district.
The Councils will oversee local development planning, health, education, tourism, infrastructure, and welfare schemes.
Each Council will have its own dedicated Council Fund.
They will have the authority to levy taxes, fees and other charges in accordance with the law.
The administration has proposed a Union Territory-level elected body to function above the seven Hill Councils.
This body will be established under a customised Article 371 framework.
Chief Secretary Kundra said this model has no parallel elsewhere in India and will draw on the best features of other constitutional arrangements.
Article 371 of the Constitution provides special safeguards and autonomy to certain states and regions to protect local interests.
These provisions aim to protect cultural identity, land rights, local employment and administrative systems.
Part XXI of the Constitution contains these special provisions, with clauses ranging from Articles 371A to 371J.
The Centre has offered constitutional safeguards under Article 371 as an alternative to the Sixth Schedule.
The proposed UT-level body would have legislative, executive, financial and administrative powers.
The framework is being designed to provide Ladakh with a more flexible and tailored form of autonomy than the standard Sixth Schedule template.

topics.title: ‘Satluj’ Movie Controversy
bullets: On 3 July 2026, the film Satluj was removed from ZEE5 just two days after its premiere.
The film depicts activist Jaswant Singh Khalra’s work during Punjab's insurgency (mid-1980s to early-1990s).
A government committee is examining it under Section 69A of the IT Act. Background –
Punjab witnessed a violent separatist movement seeking an independent Sikh state called "Khalistan" (mid-1980s to early- 1990s).
Militant groups targeted government officials, security forces, and civilians.
Security forces counter-insurgency operations were often accused of human rights violations.
The movement's roots trace to the 1947 Partition, which left Sikhs as a minority.
Leaders like Master Tara Singh advocated for a separate Sikh state.
The modern movement emerged in the 1970s after the 1966 linguistic reorganisation of Punjab.
The Anandpur Sahib Resolution, passed by the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) on 17 October 1973.
It demanded greater autonomy for the state of Punjab, identified regions that would be part of a separate state, and sought the right to frame its own internal constitution.
The movement was led most effectively by Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale.
In May 1980, Jagjit Singh Chauhan travelled to London and announced the formation of Khalistan.
A similar announcement was made by Balbir Singh Sandhu in Amritsar, who released stamps and currency of Khalistan.
On 12 April 1980, the Council of Khalistan was officially formed at Anandpur Sahib, with Chauhan declaring himself its president.
Operation Blue Star was an Indian military operation carried out from 1 to 10 June 1984 to flush out militants from the Golden Temple complex.
The operation was ordered by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi to eliminate Bhindranwale and his followers.
The operation resulted in hundreds of deaths and severely damaged the temple's inner shrine, deeply offending the Sikh community.
The Indian government launched Operation Black Thunder in 1986 and 1988 to clear militants from the Golden Temple again.
These operations were more surgical and targeted compared to Operation Blue Star.
The operations successfully flushed out militants but further deepened the trust deficit between the Sikh community and the state.
On 31 October 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her two Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh.
The assassination was an act of revenge for Operation Blue Star.
Beant Singh was shot dead at the scene, while Satwant Singh was later tried, convicted, and executed.
The 1980s saw the rise of several militant groups fighting for Khalistan, including the Khalistan Commando Force (KCF) and Babbar Khalsa International.
The KCF was formed in August 1986 with the support of the Panthic Committee and Damdami Taksal.
In 1986, the KCF took responsibility for the assassination of General Arun Vaidya, who had been the Chief of the Army Staff during Operation Blue Star.
On 31 August 1995, Punjab Chief Minister Beant Singh was assassinated in a bomb blast.
By the mid-1990s, the Khalistan insurgency had petered out.
The movement failed to reach its objectives due to a heavy police crackdown, factional infighting, and disillusionment from the Sikh population. Recent News –
Satluj (originally titled Punjab’95 ) is a Hindi-language film directed by Honey Trehan and starring Diljit Dosanjh as Jaswant Singh Khalra.
The film was produced by Rakesh Om Prakash Mehra and is based on the life of Khalra and his fight to uncover the truth about extrajudicial killings in Punjab.
The film premiered on 1 July 2026 on the ZEE5 OTT platform after years of delays over a certification dispute with the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC).
The film premiered on ZEE5 on 1 July 2026 to much anticipation.
However, just two days after its premiere (on 3 July 2026 ), the film was removed from the platform's India catalogue.
The film continues to stream internationally through ZEE5 Global, No official blocking order has been made public. Legal Framework –
Section 69A, inserted by the Information Technology (Amendment) Act, 2008, empowers the Central Government to block public access to information on computer resources.
Grounds: sovereignty, security, public order, or preventing incitement to cognisable offences.
Orders are issued by the Secretary, MeitY, under the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009.
Under Section 69A, the Central Government can issue a blocking order to any intermediary or to the public after recording reasons in writing.
The Designated Officer (Secretary, MeitY) examines the information and, if satisfied, refers the matter to the Review Committee for approval.
The Review Committee, consisting of senior government officials, reviews the case and recommends the blocking order before it is issued.
Reports suggest that a Union government-appointed committee is examining Satluj under Section 69A of the IT Act.
The committee is reportedly evaluating the film's content to determine if it violates any of the grounds for blocking under Section 69A.
The government's decision to review the film has been criticised by opposition parties and civil society as an act of censorship. Truth Commission –
A Truth Commission (or Truth and Reconciliation Commission ) is a temporary body established by a government to investigate human rights violations, war crimes, or state- sponsored abuses.
It is typically a non-judicial body that does not have legal power to initiate action against someone.
Its aim is to record statements, build an official record, and bring about national reconciliation.

According to political scientist Priscilla B. Hayner, a truth commission: ➢Is focused on the past, rather than ongoing events. ➢Engages directly and broadly with the affected population, gathering information on their experiences. ➢Is a temporary body, with the aim of concluding with a final report. ➢Is officially authorized or empowered by the state under review.
India has never had a truth commission at the national or state level.
Demands have been raised for events like the Partition, 1984 anti- Sikh riots, Kashmiri pandit exodus, and 2002 Gujarat riots.
In 2023, Justice Sanjay Kaul recommended a truth and reconciliation commission for J&K while upholding Article 370's abrogation.
At least 70 countries around the world have established truth commissions or similar bodies.
South Africa established a Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) in 1995 to uncover human rights violations during the decades of apartheid.
Canada constituted a TRC in 2008 to investigate the multi- generational trauma caused by a residential school system for indigenous children.
A truth commission is a government-sanctioned body with official authority.
A "People's Commission" has no legal sanctity – it is a private, non-official initiative.
Paramjit Kaur Khalra has demanded a "People's Commission" for Punjab, while others, including the Shiromani Akali Dal, have sought a formal "truth commission" .
A private, non-official "People's Commission for Human Rights Violation in Punjab" was constituted in 1998 after the retirement of Supreme Court judge Justice Kuldip Singh.
Its aim was to document testimonies from families of victims of extrajudicial killings.
This commission was a precursor to the current demands for a formal inquiry. Jaswant Singh Khalra –
Jaswant Singh Khalra was a human rights activist based in Punjab who worked tirelessly to document the alleged extrajudicial killings and disappearances during the insurgency.
He was a chartered accountant by profession who became a human rights crusader after witnessing the violence and state repression in Punjab.
Khalra was abducted and killed on 6 September 1995 – his body was never found.
Khalra and his team collected testimonies from families of victims who had "disappeared" or were killed in alleged fake encounters.
He documented the cremation of 2,097 unidentified bodies in Amritsar district alone – a figure that was later investigated by the CBI and found to be true.
Khalra and his wife Paramjit Kaur Khalra have always alleged that at least 25,000 people had either "disappeared" or their bodies were cremated as "unidentified" by Punjab Police.
On 6 September 1995, Khalra was abducted by plainclothes police personnel near his home in Amritsar.
He was taken to an unknown location and killed – his body was never recovered.
The killing of Khalra is widely seen as a state-sanctioned murder and remains one of the most brutal examples of the repression during the insurgency.
After Khalra's murder, his wife Paramjit Kaur Khalra took up his work and became a prominent human rights activist.
She has been demanding justice for her husband and truth about the killings during the insurgency.
She is currently calling for a "People's Commission" to investigate the human rights violations during that period.
